LE presents many of the same cryogenic storage and delivery challenges as LH or LNG. Ethane 2 boils at about −89°C (184 K) under atmospheric pressure. To keep it liquid, storage systems either cool it to cryogenic temperatures or maintain it under elevated pressure (its vapor pressure at around 20°C can reach very high values). In a bulk fueling context, the most practical solution is likely to operate at low temperatures so that the LE remains close to its boiling point while minimizing the pressure. Venting ethane has lesser impact on environment than methane due to lower global warming potential (GWP) of 5.5 a.u. (compared to 27 a.u. for methane). Handling LE is associated with significant safety challenges. LE is more volatile and flammable than LNG, its vapors are heavier than air, and it is classified as a simple asphyxiant (Stanford Linear Accelerator Center 2013). 74 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4.3 Infrastructure and Operations This subsection provides more details on possible cryogenic infrastructure configurations and operations at airports, with a particular emphasis on safety, logistic, and regulatory considerations. In Section 4.2, we briefly note how each cryogenic fuel compares in regard to storage offset distance requirements and dispensing configurations. We found each cryogenic fuel must abide by safety distance requirements while in bulk storage and that each fuel can be dispensed in a similar manner. Differences in safety distances and delivery and dispensing operations are tied primarily to different fuel characteristics. In terms of airport operations and logistics, volumetric energy density is one of the more important fuel characteristics because it impacts how much space is required for storage and impacts how much energy can be delivered (to the airport or to aircraft) in a single truck load. In the case of leakage events, contact with skin and possible fuel ignition are two of the main safety risks. 4.3.1 Cryogenic Hydrogen This section provides insights on the space requirements for LH infrastructure at an airport and 2 gives examples of refueling and operating procedures that may take place at airports in the future. It also notes where knowledge gaps exist and where standardized procedures are still needed before LH -powered flight can become a reality. This section primarily leverages 2 information from IATA’s Concept of Operations of Battery and Hydrogen-Powered Aircraft at Aerodromes report (Airport Compatibility of Alternative Aviation Fuels Task Force, International Industry Working Group 2025) and NLR’s Hydrogen Infrastructure Analysis Frameworks for Aviation Applications report (Bracci et al. 2026).
